Node colors mark the classes that neighborhood aggregation finds: the degree-3 node (C, x) in accent, the two other triangle nodes (A, B and y, z) in teal, and the tail end (D, w) in violet. Both graphs reduce to the same class counts, so the card shows the same hash, starting c0454391, for each, and equal is True." width="100%"} The Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) hash summarizes a graph's structure in a short hexadecimal string. Isomorphic graphs always get the same hash, so different hashes prove that two graphs differ. The converse does not hold: some non-isomorphic graphs (for example many regular graphs of the same degree) share a hash. It is the standard way to group or deduplicate large collections of graphs, such as molecules, before running exact isomorphism tests within each group, and it underlies the WL graph kernels used in machine learning. Each node starts with a label (its degree, or the attribute named by `node_attr=`), then, `iterations` times, replaces it by a hash of its own label and the sorted labels of its neighbors (prefixed by the edge attribute named by `edge_attr=`, if given). The graph hash is a hash of the counts of labels across all rounds. The result is identical to NetworkX's `weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash` for the same graph (NetworkX 3.5 or later), except for directed graphs hashed with `edge_attr=`. There, each neighbor label keeps its successor or predecessor prefix, following the fix in NetworkX pull request #8946. NetworkX releases without that fix drop the prefix, so an in-star and an out-star get the same hash. Parallel edges count once and a self-loop makes a node its own neighbor, as in a NetworkX `Graph` or `DiGraph`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional node attribute used as the initial label (converted with `str()`). Every node must have it. [edge_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional edge attribute whose value prefixes each neighbor's label. Every edge must have it. [iterations]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[3]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of neighborhood aggregation rounds (default 3). More rounds look further from each node. [digest_size]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[16]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Size of the BLAKE2b digests, in bytes (the hash string has twice as many hex characters). Default 16. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The hash, as a hexadecimal string. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `iterations` is not positive, or a node or edge lacks a named attribute. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} This is the WL subtree hash of Shervashidze et al. (2011). With degree labels, the first round only re-encodes the degrees, so NetworkX (and this method) runs one round fewer in that case. Each round costs $O(E \log \Delta)$ for sorting neighbor labels. Two graphs get equal hashes exactly when 1-WL color refinement cannot tell them apart within the given number of rounds (barring hash collisions). ## Examples {.doc-examples} Relabeling a graph does not change its hash: ::: {#fd0bfd85 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec a = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) a.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D")]) b = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["w", "x", "y", "z"]) b.add_edges([("z", "y"), ("y", "x"), ("x", "z"), ("w", "x")]) a.weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash() == b.weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Equal hashes are not proof of isomorphism. A six-node cycle and two triangles are both 2-regular, so neighborhood aggregation never tells their nodes apart and the hashes collide, while `is_isomorphic()` sees the difference: ::: {#1ccfb4a5 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} hexagon = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(6) two_triangles = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(3).add_cycle_graph(3) ( hexagon.weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash() == two_triangles.weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash(), hexagon.is_isomorphic(two_triangles), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: :::
